rationale: A wins because it knows where the story is strong and where it becomes a lawsuit-shaped hole. Its labor angle says the hard part plainly: "the split between roles cut and roles left unfilled — without it this angle is unpitchable." B opens with "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone," which turns a workload-equivalent metric into a headcount claim the update does not support. That is not edge; that is a fact-check bill arriving early.
gaps_in_A: "The other third got harder" is a smart operations angle, but it is still an inference; the update does not say the remaining human-handled chats became harder.
"the humans keep a caseload that is now entirely the hard third" overstates the evidence. A correctly asks for residual-caseload data, but the headline framing gets ahead of the supplied facts.
"Klarna heads for an IPO with two-thirds of its support desk automated" blurs chats into the whole support desk. The update says two-thirds of customer-service chats, not two-thirds of the function.
gaps_in_B: "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" is the central foul. The update says the AI handled equivalent work, not that 700 people left or were eliminated.
"advocacy concerns surfacing now are likely to precede regulatory attention" invents timing and regulatory momentum. The update only says some consumer advocates raised concerns.
"The Headcount It Cut Is the Margin It's Showing Investors" overclaims causality. The facts do not say the IPO margin story comes from AI-driven headcount cuts.
"Every Bank and Payments Company Now Has a Public Benchmark" is too grand for the evidence. Klarna disclosed a metric; the update does not prove competitors will treat it as an industry benchmark.
